title: Why a Slow Off Switch Can Count

scenes.tts: How can a cell count? Calcium often rises in brief spikes. In many cell types, a stronger stimulus gives more frequent spikes of about the same height. To read that, a cell needs a part that switches on fast and off slowly.
scenes.visual: A dashed question box sits below two calcium spike trains: a weaker stimulus with few spikes, a stronger one with more, all of about the same height. The box becomes a decoder chip tagged 'on fast' and 'off slowly'.
scenes.narration: How can a cell count? Calcium often rises in brief spikes. In many cell types, a stronger stimulus gives more frequent spikes of about the same height. To read that, a cell needs a part that switches on fast and off slowly.

scenes.tts: Picture a bucket with a small hole, topped up by one cup of water at each spike. Fill it rarely, and it drains between cups. Fill it often, and the level climbs.
scenes.visual: Two idealised buckets with a small hole. Left: a cup falls rarely and the level drains back between cups. Right: cups fall often and the level climbs.
scenes.narration: Picture a bucket with a small hole, topped up by one cup of water at each spike. Fill it rarely, and it drains between cups. Fill it often, and the level climbs.

scenes.tts: Take a decoder that loses its activity with a fixed half-time. The fraction left at the next spike is one half, raised to the gap between spikes divided by the half-time. With a half-time of 20 seconds, spikes a minute apart leave one eighth of the activity. Spikes 10 seconds apart leave about 70 percent to build on.

scenes.tts: In 1998, Ricardo Dolmetsch, Keli Xu and Richard Lewis tested human T cells. They imposed calcium spikes of chosen spacing on a line of these cells. Closely spaced spikes activated three transcription factors, N F A T and N F kappa B among them. Widely spaced spikes activated only N F kappa B. A likely reason is how fast each one switches off. N F A T leaves the nucleus within minutes once calcium falls. In B cells, N F kappa B was found to stay in the nucleus. It stayed for more than 16 minutes after a brief calcium spike. So a decoder that holds on between spikes can count.
